checks.title: What we check
checks.intro: Every check follows a fixed, public rule. Here is what we look for.

duplicates.title: Duplicate charges
duplicates.body: The same service billed more than once on the same day.

math.title: Math errors
math.body: Units times price that does not match the amount charged.

dates.title: Wrong dates
dates.body: Charges dated outside the time you were actually there.

unbundling.title: Unbundling
unbundling.body: Parts of one procedure billed separately when they should be billed together.

quantity.title: Quantity limits
quantity.body: More units billed than Medicare allows for a single visit.

outliers.title: Price outliers
outliers.body: Prices far above what Medicare pays for the same service.

vague.title: Vague charges
vague.body: Lump-sum or unlabeled charges that do not say what they were for.

denied.title: Denied, then billed
denied.body: Insurance denied a service, but you were billed the full amount. Needs your insurer's EOB.

balance.title: Balance billing
balance.body: The bill asks you to pay more than your insurer's EOB says you owe. Needs your insurer's EOB.

trust.title: Findings come from public Medicare rules, not from AI guessing.
trust.subtitle: AI only reads your bill.
trust.body: A fixed set of checks built on public Medicare rules decides what gets flagged, and the wording of each finding comes from fixed templates. The AI never decides what is wrong. It only turns your bill into structured data and, if you tap “What is this?” on a line, defines that one billing code.

Report.title: Your report
Report.subtitle: Here is what our fixed checks flagged on your bill.
Report.honest: These are things worth asking about, not certain mistakes.

empty.title: We did not find anything worth asking about
empty.body: Every check that applied to your bill ran, and none of them flagged a concern. Some checks only cover services on the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule, so the price, quantity-limit and unbundling checks skipped any line that is not on it, such as hospital facility charges, lab tests and anesthesia. The two checks that need an EOB ran only if you uploaded one. These checks cannot catch everything, so if something still looks wrong to you, it is fine to ask the billing office.

rules.math_error: Charge does not match units times price
rules.ncci_unbundling: Possibly billed separately when it should be together
rules.denied_billed_in_full: Denied by insurance, then billed to you

why.duplicateCharge: The same service, with the same code, date, units, and price, appears more than once on your bill. Sometimes a service really is done twice, but it is worth confirming.
why.mathError: The charge is higher than the units multiplied by the unit price shown on the same line, so the numbers on this line do not add up.
why.dateMismatch: This charge is dated outside the dates of service printed on your bill, so it may belong to a different visit or have a typing error.
why.ncciNever: Medicare's coding rules say these two services should be billed together as one, and no modifier is allowed to split them. Billing both can mean paying twice for the same work.
why.ncciModifier: Medicare's coding rules say these two services are normally billed together as one. They may be billed separately only when a modifier shows they were truly distinct, so it is worth asking why they were split.
why.mueLine: Medicare sets a limit on how many units of this service can be billed on one line. This bill shows more than that limit.
why.mueDayPolicy: Medicare sets a firm limit on how many units of this service can be billed for one patient on one day. This bill shows more than that limit.
why.mueDayClinical: Medicare sets a typical limit on how many units of this service are billed for one patient on one day. Going over can be valid with medical documentation, so it is worth asking.
why.priceOutlier: This price is more than five times what Medicare pays for the same service in Los Angeles. Providers can charge more than Medicare, so this is a reason to ask, not proof of an error.
why.vagueCharge: This line does not say what service it was for, such as a lump sum or a charge with no code. You can ask for an itemized explanation.
why.deniedBilled: Your insurance denied this service, but the bill asks you to pay the full amount. It is worth asking whether the denial was appealed or the amount is correct.
why.fallback: A fixed check on your bill's line items flagged this. Ask the billing office to explain the charge.
why.balanceBilling: Your insurer's Explanation of Benefits says you owe less for this service than the bill asks you to pay. The difference may be a payment or adjustment that has not shown up on the bill yet, so it is worth asking before you pay.

Report.disclaimer: This report points out charges that may be worth asking about. It is not legal or medical advice, and it cannot confirm that any charge is wrong. Please check with the billing office before relying on it.

doc.subject: Request for an itemized bill and review of specific charges
doc.intro: I am writing to better understand the charges on my recent bill. Please send me a complete itemized bill that lists each service with its billing code, date, and charge. I would also appreciate a review of the {count, plural, one {item} other {items}} listed below, which I have questions about.

duplicateCharge.firm: Could you confirm whether this service was performed more than once on this date? The same code, date, units, and price appear more than once on my bill.
duplicateCharge.soft: This may be correct, but this line looks the same as another one. Could you please check whether this service was billed twice?

mathError.firm: Could you explain how this charge was calculated? It is higher than the units multiplied by the unit price shown on the same line.
mathError.soft: Could you please check how this charge was calculated? It may be higher than the units multiplied by the unit price shown on this line.

dateMismatch.firm: Could you confirm the date of this service? It is dated outside the dates of service shown on my bill.
dateMismatch.soft: Could you please check the date of this service? It may fall outside the dates of service shown on my bill.

ncciNever.firm: Could you explain why this service was billed separately from a related service? Medicare coding rules appear to bundle the two together.
ncciNever.soft: Could you please check whether this service should have been billed together with a related service under Medicare coding rules?

ncciModifier.firm: Could you explain why this service was billed separately from a related service? Medicare coding rules normally bundle them unless a modifier shows they were distinct.
ncciModifier.soft: Could you please confirm whether this service was truly distinct from a related service, or whether it should have been billed together with it?

mueLine.firm: Could you confirm the number of units billed? It appears to be above the Medicare limit for a single line.
mueLine.soft: Could you please check the number of units billed? It may be above the Medicare limit for a single line.

mueDayPolicy.firm: Could you confirm the number of units billed for this day? It appears to be above the Medicare daily limit for this service.
mueDayPolicy.soft: Could you please check the number of units billed for this day? It may be above the Medicare daily limit for this service.

mueDayClinical.firm: Could you share the documentation that supports the number of units billed for this day? It appears to be above the usual Medicare daily limit for this service.
mueDayClinical.soft: Could you please confirm the number of units billed for this day? It may be above the usual Medicare daily limit for this service.

priceOutlier.firm: Could you explain how this price was set? It is more than five times what Medicare pays for the same service.
priceOutlier.soft: Could you please tell me how this price was set? It may be well above what Medicare pays for the same service.

vagueCharge.firm: Could you provide an itemized description of what this charge covers? My bill does not say which service it was for.
vagueCharge.soft: Could you please describe which service this charge covers? I could not tell from my bill.

deniedBilled.firm: My insurance appears to have denied this service. Could you explain why it is being billed to me in full, and whether an appeal was filed?
deniedBilled.soft: My insurance may have denied this service. Could you please confirm whether it should be billed to me in full?

fallback.firm: Could you please explain this charge and confirm that it is correct?
fallback.soft: Could you please double-check this charge?

balanceBilling.firm: My insurer's Explanation of Benefits shows a lower amount owed for this service than my bill asks me to pay. Could you explain the difference and send me a corrected statement?
balanceBilling.soft: My insurer's Explanation of Benefits may show a lower amount owed for this service than my bill. Could you please check whether the amount I am being asked to pay is correct?

doc.response: I would be grateful for a written response within 30 days of receiving this letter. If any of these charges are correct, an explanation of the service and its billing code would be very helpful.
doc.closing: Thank you for your time and help.
doc.footer: This letter was prepared with Unbundle and is not legal advice.

Privacy.title: Privacy Policy

summary.title: In short
summary.files: Your files are stored in a private folder that only your account can read, write or delete.
summary.browser: Our upload form resizes photos in your browser before they are uploaded.
summary.anthropic: Your files are sent to Anthropic's API so your bill can be read. The only other thing sent is a single billing code, and only if you open “What is this?” on a line. If you type your bill in instead of uploading it, nothing you type is sent to Anthropic, apart from that same billing code. Anthropic's published terms say that, by default, your bills aren't used to train its models and API data is deleted within 30 days. Those are Anthropic's terms, not ours.
summary.delete: Deleting a bill removes the bill, its line items and the uploaded files from our storage.
summary.storage: We use a language cookie only if you choose a language, session cookies when you sign in, and your light or dark choice in your browser's local storage. We do not use analytics, advertising or tracking cookies.

Privacy.intro: Unbundle is a student project built for the Congressional App Challenge. It helps people check their medical bills. This page explains what information we collect and what we do with it.

collect.title: What we collect
collect.email: Your Google account email and name, so you can sign in.
collect.files: The files you upload: a photo or PDF of your bill and, optionally, your insurer's Explanation of Benefits.
collect.items: The line items, dates, codes and amounts we read from those files, or that you type in yourself, and any changes you make to them.

files.title: What happens to your uploaded files
files.private: Files are stored in a private Supabase storage bucket, in a folder that only your account can read, write or delete.
files.resized: Our upload form resizes photos and re-saves them as JPEG in your browser before they are uploaded, so the copy we store is normally smaller than the original and no longer carries its camera metadata. PDFs are uploaded as they are, and our upload form turns away PDFs over 4 MB. These steps happen in your browser, so our server does not enforce them: it accepts files up to the limit below and does not re-save images itself.
files.checked: We check each file's actual type, size (10 MB) and, for PDFs, page count (6) before storing it. Only JPEG, PNG, WebP and PDF files are accepted.
files.use: We use your files only to read your bill. We do not use them to train models or for advertising.

anthropic.title: How Anthropic is involved
anthropic.body: To read the text on your bill, our server sends your uploaded files to Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, through Anthropic's API. Anthropic processes the images to read them and returns the line items. The model only reads what is printed; it does not decide whether a charge is wrong. Those checks are run by fixed rules in our own code. Anthropic's published commercial terms say it may not train its models on customer content sent through its services, and its API data policy says that, by default, it automatically deletes API inputs and outputs from its systems within 30 days, except where content is flagged for violating its usage policy or the law requires it to keep it longer. Those are Anthropic's terms, not ours, and they can change; see <link>Anthropic's retention policy</link>. If you open “What is this?” on a line, only that line's billing code (for example, 99213) is sent for a general explanation, never your name, dates, or amounts. If you type your bill in instead of uploading it, what you type is not sent to Anthropic at all; it is saved to your account and checked by our own fixed rules. Our API key is kept on the server and never sent to your browser.

kept.title: Where it is kept
kept.body: Your bills, line items and files are stored in Supabase (our database and file storage), and access is limited to your account by row-level security. There is no retention period and nothing expires on its own: we keep them until you delete them. We don't put bill contents in our logs.

cookies.title: Cookies and browser storage
cookies.language: Language: if you choose a language with the EN | ES switch, we save that choice in a cookie named NEXT_LOCALE. It holds only “en” or “es” and lasts one year. If you never choose, no language cookie is set and pages follow your browser's language setting.
cookies.signin: Signing in: when you sign in, our sign-in provider, Supabase, sets session cookies on this site to keep you signed in. They last up to 400 days, and signing out removes them. Browsing without signing in sets no session cookies.
cookies.theme: Appearance: if you choose Light or Dark, we save that choice in your browser's local storage under the name unbundle-theme. Choosing System removes it. It stays in your browser.
cookies.none: We do not use analytics, advertising or tracking cookies.

dont.title: What we don't do
dont.body: We never sell your information. We share it only with the services that process it for us: Anthropic, which reads your uploaded files as described above; Supabase, which stores your account, bills and files; Google, which handles sign-in; and our web hosting provider, which serves the site and runs our server code.

delete.title: Deleting your data
delete.body: From Settings you can do two things. “Delete all my bills” permanently removes every bill you uploaded, the line items and EOB lines we stored for them, and your uploaded files from storage; your account stays. “Delete my account and data” does the same and then removes your sign-in account from our authentication system and signs you out, so the data tied to your account is removed from our database and storage. You can also delete a single bill from your dashboard or its review page. Findings are not stored: they are worked out from your line items each time you open a report, so there is nothing to delete for them. Deleting a bill leaves one thing behind: a record that a reading was attempted (your user ID and a timestamp, with no bill content), which we keep until you delete your account and use to apply hourly limits. Deleting does not recall copies Anthropic may keep under its own retention policy, and a PDF letter you already downloaded stays on your device.

About.title: About Unbundle
About.subtitle: A free tool that checks a medical bill against public Medicare rules and gives you a letter to take to the billing office.

what.title: What Unbundle is
what.line1: A family gets a hospital bill they can't verify.
what.line2: Unbundle checks it against public Medicare rules.
what.line3: They get a letter that says what is worth asking about.

how.title: How it works
how.intro: The AI only reads your bill into structured data. It never decides what is wrong. Every finding comes from fixed, tested rules built on public data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS):
how.ncci: NCCI procedure-to-procedure edits, which list services that should not be billed together
how.mue: medically unlikely edits, which cap how many units of a service make sense in one visit
how.mpfs: the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule, which sets what Medicare pays for each service
how.explain: The AI does two small jobs: it reads your bill into structured data, and if you tap “What is this?” on a line, it defines that single billing code in general terms. Fixed code decides every finding, and the wording of each finding comes from fixed templates. The AI cannot add, remove or change a finding or its amount.

Two run only if you upload your insurer's Explanation of Benefits (EOB): Denied, then billed and Balance billing. Balance billing compares what the bill asks you to pay with what the EOB says you owe.

Help.title: Help and common questions
Help.subtitle: Plain answers to what people ask most.

links.about: How the checks work and how we tested them

legal.a: No. Unbundle is not legal or medical advice. It points out charges that may be worth asking about, using fixed checks built on public Medicare rules. A findings list is a reason to ask the billing office a question, not proof of a mistake. For advice about your rights, a lawyer or a patient advocate can help.

bills.q: What kinds of bills does it work on?
bills.a: Itemized bills and statements from doctors' offices, clinics, and other providers, as a photo or a PDF, or typed in by hand if you have no photo. The price and quantity checks use Medicare's physician fee schedule for Los Angeles, so they fit services on that schedule best. Hospital facility charges, such as a room fee, are outside what the price checks cover. A bill with one lump sum and no line items can't be checked, so ask the billing office for an itemized bill first.

accuracy.a: We ran the checks against {fixtures} made-up test bills, including {traps} designed to catch false alarms, and they behaved as designed. Real bills are messier, so some problems will be missed and some flags will turn out to be fine. That is why every finding says what to ask rather than what is wrong.

cost.a: Unbundle is free to use, including the report and the letter.

eob.a: An Explanation of Benefits is a statement from your insurance company. It is not a bill. It shows what the provider charged, what your plan allowed and paid, and what you may owe. If you add one when you upload, Unbundle compares it with your bill.

unbundling.a: Some services are meant to be billed together as one charge. Unbundling is billing the pieces separately, which can add up to more. Medicare publishes pairs of codes that normally should not be billed together, and Unbundle flags those pairs so you can ask why they were split.

uninsured.q: What if I don't have insurance?
uninsured.a: Ask for an itemized bill and for the provider's financial assistance policy and application, since many hospitals reduce bills based on income. If you were given a Good Faith Estimate before your care, you can compare it with your bill in the financial help step. You can also ask about prompt-pay discounts and payment plans, and ask that your account not go to collections while it is reviewed.

Methodology.title: How the checks work
Methodology.subtitle: Nine fixed checks, each written in code. This page says what each one does, when it stays quiet, and what data it uses.
Methodology.intro: Every finding comes from one of these checks. The AI only reads your bill into structured data; fixed, tested rules decide every finding. Separately, it can give a general definition of a billing code when you ask. It never decides whether something is a problem.

duplicate_charge.name: Duplicate charge
duplicate_charge.what: Two or more lines with the same code, date of service, modifiers, units, unit price and charge.
duplicate_charge.skips: Lines with no code, no date, or a charge of zero or less are never compared.
duplicate_charge.confidence: Medium. Some services really are done twice.
duplicate_charge.example: Code 80053 appears twice on March 2, 1 unit, $40.00 each. One extra copy: $40.00 in question.

math_error.name: Math error
math_error.what: A line whose charge is more than its units multiplied by its unit price.
math_error.skips: Lines with no unit price or a negative one. A charge below units times price is not flagged.
math_error.example: 2 units at $50.00 should be $100.00, but the charge is $130.00. $30.00 in question.

date_mismatch.name: Date outside the service range
date_mismatch.what: A line dated before the start or after the end of the service dates printed on the statement.
date_mismatch.skips: No check if the statement has no dates, or if its start date is after its end date.
date_mismatch.example: The statement covers March 1 to March 3, but one line is dated March 9. That line's full charge is in question.

ncci_unbundling.name: Possible unbundling
ncci_unbundling.what: Two lines on the same date that a Medicare NCCI procedure-to-procedure edit says should not be billed together, because one is normally included in the other.
ncci_unbundling.skips: When the edit allows a modifier and the bundled line carries one of 59, XE, XP, XS or XU, or modifier 25 on an evaluation and management (E/M) code (99202 to 99499). No check for hospital (facility) edits.
ncci_unbundling.confidence: High when the edit allows no modifier at all. Medium when a modifier could have been used.
ncci_unbundling.example: An edit lists code A as the main service and code B as included in it. Both are billed on the same day, and B has no modifier. B's charge is in question.

mue_exceeded.name: More units than Medicare expects
mue_exceeded.what: The units billed for one code on one date, added across all lines, are above Medicare's medically unlikely edit (MUE) for that code.
mue_exceeded.skips: A total equal to the limit. Codes with no MUE. Lines with no code or date.
mue_exceeded.confidence: High for date-of-service edits. Medium when the edit applies per claim line, since adding lines is less certain.
mue_exceeded.example: A code has a limit of 1 unit per day and is billed at 3 units. The 2 extra units at their unit price are in question.

price_outlier.name: Price far above Medicare
price_outlier.what: A unit charge for a CPT or HCPCS code that is more than 5 times the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule price for Los Angeles (locality 18), office setting.
price_outlier.skips: Exactly 5 times does not fire. Codes with no Medicare price, services not on the schedule, and lines with no code.
price_outlier.confidence: Medium. Medicare is a benchmark, not what your provider agreed to with your plan. The 5-times line is our own choice, not a legal limit.
price_outlier.example: Medicare's price for a service is $20.00 and the bill charges $150.00. That is over $100.00 (5 times), so the $130.00 difference is in question.

vague_charge.name: Vague charge
vague_charge.what: A line with no code whose description is a generic word (misc, miscellaneous, other, supplies, services, pharmacy, general), or an uncoded line over $100.00.
vague_charge.skips: Any line that has a code. Lines with a charge of zero or less.
vague_charge.example: A line reads 'Misc supplies' with no code and a charge of $45.00. The full $45.00 is in question.

denied_billed_in_full.name: Denied by insurance but billed to you
denied_billed_in_full.what: Your insurer's explanation of benefits (EOB) shows a denial reason for a service, and the bill still asks you to pay for the same code and date.
denied_billed_in_full.skips: Needs an EOB. EOB lines without a code or date are not matched. A line where you owe nothing.
denied_billed_in_full.confidence: High. A denial can be correct, so read the denial reason on your EOB.
denied_billed_in_full.example: The EOB denies a code on April 5 and the bill still shows $75.00 owed by you. $75.00 is in question.

balance_billing.name: Bill asks for more than the EOB says you owe
balance_billing.what: The bill's patient amount for a service is higher than the patient responsibility on the EOB for the same code and date.
balance_billing.skips: Needs an EOB. Only when exactly one bill line and one EOB line match. Denied lines (a separate check). Lines where either amount is unknown.
balance_billing.confidence: Medium. The bill and the EOB are made at different times, so the gap may be a payment not yet shown.
balance_billing.example: The bill says you owe $120.00 and the EOB says your share is $50.00. The $70.00 difference is in question.

data.ncciPtp: NCCI procedure-to-procedure edits: practitioner edits only (edit set 1), 2026 Q4 release.
data.ncciMue: NCCI medically unlikely edits: practitioner services table, 2026 Q4 release.
data.mpfs: Medicare Physician Fee Schedule relative value units: RVU26A.
data.locality: Locality: Los Angeles, Medicare administrative contractor 01182, locality 18. Other places are not covered.
data.conversion: Conversion factor: the standard one, not the one for qualifying alternative payment model participants.
data.setting: Setting: office (non-facility) prices, with the 26 and TC modifier rows where they exist.

limits.scope: Price and quantity checks only cover services that are on the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule. Hospital facility charges, such as a room fee, are outside them.
limits.test: We tested the checks on made-up bills written alongside the rules, so the results show agreement with our own expectations, not real-world accuracy.
limits.advice: A finding is a reason to ask a question, not proof of a mistake, and not legal advice.

Glossary.title: Glossary
Glossary.subtitle: Plain words for the terms you will see on bills and reports.
Glossary.attribution: CPT® is a registered trademark of the American Medical Association. The explanations on this page are our own plain-language descriptions.

allowedAmount.definition: The most your plan or Medicare will count for a service. It can be lower than what the provider charged.

balanceBilling.definition: When a provider bills you for the difference between its charge and what your insurer allowed or paid. Whether that is permitted depends on the plan, the contract and the law. Unbundle only compares what the bill asks you to pay with what your EOB says you owe.

cpt.definition: A five-character code that names a medical service or procedure, such as a visit, a test or a treatment. CPT is maintained by the American Medical Association.

eob.definition: A statement from your insurer that shows what it was charged, what it allowed and paid, what it denied, and what you may owe. It is not a bill.

financialAssistance.definition: A hospital program that reduces or removes a bill for people who cannot pay in full. It is also called charity care. Each hospital has its own policy.

fpl.definition: Yearly income figures published by the federal government by household size. Financial assistance programs often use a percentage of it.

gfe.definition: A written estimate of what care is expected to cost, given before the care. It is meant for people who are uninsured or paying themselves.

gpci.definition: A number that adjusts Medicare's price for a service to local costs. Unbundle uses the one for Los Angeles.

hcpcs.definition: The wider set of billing codes used with Medicare. It includes CPT codes and also codes, usually a letter and four digits, for supplies, equipment and other services.

itemizedBill.definition: A bill that lists every service and supply on its own line, with its billing code, date, units and charge.

modifier.definition: A two-character add-on to a billing code that gives more detail, for example 25, 26, 59 or TC. Some modifiers show that two services were truly separate.

mpfs.definition: The list of what Medicare pays for services by doctors and other practitioners. Unbundle uses it as a price benchmark.

mue.definition: The most units of a service that Medicare would normally expect for one patient on one day.

ncci.definition: Medicare coding edits that keep some codes from being paid together or in large quantities.

patientResponsibility.definition: The part of a claim your insurer says is yours to pay, such as a deductible, a copay or coinsurance.

ptp.definition: An NCCI rule that says two codes should not normally be billed together on the same day, because one is included in the other. Some allow a modifier to show the services were separate.

unbundling.definition: Billing separately for services that should be billed together as one.

CallScript.title: Phone script
CallScript.intro: Read this when you call the billing office. It is made from your findings on this page and is not saved.
CallScript.genericIntro: A script you can adapt. When you have a report, it fills in your own findings.
CallScript.copyFailed: Could not copy. Select the text and copy it.
CallScript.opening: Hello. I'm calling about my bill. I'd like to ask about some charges. Please write down the date and your name, and I'll note mine.
CallScript.generic:
1. Ask for an itemized bill that shows a billing code for every charge.
2. Ask them to explain any charge you don't understand.
3. Ask for the financial assistance policy and application.
4. Ask that the account not go to collections while the bill is reviewed.
CallScript.closing: Before we hang up: please tell me when I can expect an answer, and who I should ask for when I call back.

ask.duplicateCharge: Why does this appear more than once with the same date, units and price?
ask.mathError: The charge is more than the units times the unit price. How was it worked out?
ask.dateMismatch: This is dated outside the service dates on the statement. Which visit does it belong to?
ask.ncciNever: Medicare coding rules say these two services shouldn't be billed together. Why were both billed?
ask.ncciModifier: Medicare coding rules say these two are normally billed together. What shows they were separate services?
ask.mueLine: The units on this line are above Medicare's limit for one line. Can you confirm the units?
ask.mueDayPolicy: The units for this day are above Medicare's firm limit. Can you confirm the units?
ask.mueDayClinical: The units for this day are above Medicare's usual limit. Is there documentation for the extra units?
ask.priceOutlier: This price is far above what Medicare pays for the same service. How is it set, and is a lower rate available?
ask.vagueCharge: I can't tell what this charge is for. What service or supply is it, and what is its billing code?
ask.deniedBilled: My insurer denied this service, but I'm being charged for it. Why am I being billed?
ask.balanceBilling: My insurer's statement says I owe less than this bill shows. Can you reconcile the two?

assistance.title: Financial assistance at a California hospital
assistance.what: California hospitals have programs that reduce or remove a bill for patients who cannot pay in full. A California law, AB 1020, raised the income level the law covers from 350% to 400% of the federal poverty level, starting January 1, 2024.
assistance.who: Whether you qualify, and whether your care is free or discounted, is decided by each hospital's own policy. Ask the hospital for it.
assistance.gap: We could not confirm from the official pages who qualifies or the exact free-care and discount levels, so we do not state them here.

steps.ask: Ask the billing office for the hospital's financial assistance policy and the application, even if you are not sure you qualify.

steps.hold: Ask that the bill not be sent to collections while your application is being reviewed, and ask them to note that on your account.

gfe.title: The Good Faith Estimate and the federal dispute process
gfe.what: A Good Faith Estimate is a written estimate of what care is expected to cost, given before the care. It is meant for people who are uninsured or paying themselves.
gfe.who: The federal patient-provider dispute resolution process is for uninsured or self-pay people who received a Good Faith Estimate and told the provider they were uninsured or not using insurance. It looks at bills that are at least $400 more than the estimate. You must start within 120 calendar days of the date of the initial bill, and there is a $25 non-refundable administrative fee.
gfe.gap: CMS decides whether a dispute qualifies. Our tool only compares your numbers with the $400 and 120-day figures CMS publishes.

steps.compare: Find your Good Faith Estimate and your bill and compare the totals.
steps.date: Check the date of the bill and count 120 calendar days from it.
steps.tool: Use the estimate tool to compare the two totals and see whether you are inside the window.
steps.start: If it applies, start the dispute on the CMS page below.

itemized.title: Asking for an itemized bill
itemized.what: An itemized bill lists every service and supply with its billing code, date, units and charge. It is what you need to check a bill line by line.
itemized.medicare: If you have Medicare: federal law lets you send a written request to a physician, provider or supplier for an itemized statement of the Medicare items and services you received. The statute says it must be furnished within 30 days of your request, and sets a civil money penalty of up to $100 for each knowing failure to do so.
itemized.other: If you do not have Medicare: we did not find an official page we could cite that sets a right to an itemized bill for private-insurance or self-pay patients, so we do not claim one. You can still ask. Contact your provider or your insurer and ask for an itemized bill with a billing code for every charge.

steps.writing: Ask in writing if you can, and keep a copy.
steps.detail: Say what you want: every service and supply, with its billing code, date, units and charge.
steps.notes: If you call, write down the date, the time and the name of the person you spoke with.
steps.letter: See what an itemized-bill letter looks like.

Checklist.title: Checklist before you dispute a bill
Checklist.subtitle: Have these in front of you before you call or write to the billing office. It makes the call shorter and your notes easier to keep.
Checklist.nothingSaved: This page has no form and keeps nothing. Print it or keep it open while you gather things.

itemized.title: The itemized bill
itemized.body: A bill that lists each charge with its billing code, date, units and amount. If all you have is a statement with one total, ask the billing office for an itemized bill.

eob.title: Your insurer's explanation of benefits (EOB)
eob.body: If you have insurance, the EOB for the same visit. It shows what the insurer was charged, what it allowed and paid, what it denied, and what you may owe.

dates.title: The dates of service
dates.body: Each date you were seen, and the date printed on the statement.

account.title: Your account number
account.body: Usually printed on the bill. The billing office may ask for it when you call.

member.title: Your insurer member ID
member.body: On your insurance card, if you have insurance.

Checklist.notesBody: For each call, write down the date, the time, the name of the person you spoke with, and what they said they would do.
Checklist.letterBody: When you are ready to ask in writing, see what an itemized-bill request letter looks like.
Checklist.letterLink: See a sample itemized-bill request letter
Checklist.rightsLink: Read about what you can ask for
Checklist.notAdvice: This checklist is general information, not legal advice.

itemized.q: What is an itemized bill, and can I ask for one?
itemized.p1: An itemized bill lists each service and supply on its own line, with its billing code, date, units and charge.
itemized.p2: If you have Medicare, federal law lets you send a written request to a physician, provider or supplier for an itemized statement of the Medicare items and services you received. It says the statement must be furnished within 30 days of your request, and sets a civil money penalty of up to $100 for each knowing failure to do so.
itemized.p3: If you do not have Medicare, we did not find an official page we could cite that sets this right, so we do not claim one. You can still ask your provider or insurer for an itemized bill.

eob.q: What is an EOB, and is it a bill?
eob.p1: An explanation of benefits (EOB) is a summary that your health plan may send after you get care. CMS says plainly that it is not a bill.
eob.p2: It shows what your provider is charging the plan and the amount the plan will cover. If the plan does not cover the whole cost, the provider may send you a separate bill, unless the law prohibits it.

allowed.p1: The allowed amount is the most your plan will pay for a covered item or service. It is generally the basis for working out your share of the cost.
allowed.p2: CMS's examples show it can be lower than what the provider billed the plan.

balanceBill.p1: If you have coverage and get care from an out-of-network provider, your plan might not cover the whole cost. The provider could then ask you to pay the difference between its charge and what your plan covers. CMS calls this a balance bill or a surprise bill.
balanceBill.p2: CMS says the federal No Surprises Act prohibits surprise billing in some circumstances. The page we cite does not list them, so we do not try to say which ones.

gfe.q: What is a Good Faith Estimate?
gfe.p1: A Good Faith Estimate is a list of expected charges, given before you get care.
gfe.p2: CMS says that in most cases providers and facilities must give you one when you schedule care at least 3 business days ahead, or if you ask for one. It is meant for people who do not have or are not using health insurance.

gfeDispute.q: Can I dispute a bill that is much higher than my estimate?
gfeDispute.p1: CMS describes a federal dispute process for people who did not have or did not use insurance and told the provider so before getting care. It applies when a provider charged at least $400 more than its Good Faith Estimate.
gfeDispute.p2: You need an initial bill dated within the last 120 calendar days, and there is a $25 non-refundable administrative fee.
gfeDispute.p3: CMS words the time limit slightly differently on different pages, so confirm your date with CMS before you rely on it. You can compare your own numbers on our estimate tool.

californiaAid.q: Is there help paying a California hospital bill?
californiaAid.p1: California's Hospital Fair Billing Program is run by HCAI. Its page says that AB 1020 raised the income level for financial assistance from 350 percent to 400 percent of the federal poverty level.
californiaAid.p2: Whether you qualify, and whether care is free or discounted, depends on the hospital's own financial assistance policy, which you can ask the billing office for. We could not confirm more detail from the official pages, so we do not state any.

mue.q: What is a medically unlikely edit (MUE)?
mue.p1: CMS defines an MUE as the maximum units of service reported for a code on the vast majority of appropriately reported claims, by the same provider for the same patient on the same date of service.
mue.p2: Not every code has one, and CMS keeps some values confidential. When the units on a bill are above a published value, Unbundle shows it as a question to ask, not as proof of an error.

ptp.q: What is a procedure-to-procedure (PTP) edit, and what is “possible unbundling”?
ptp.p1: A PTP edit is a pair of codes that CMS says should not be reported together. For the same patient on the same date, CMS says the first code of the pair (Column One) is eligible for payment and the second (Column Two) is denied, unless a clinically appropriate modifier is reported.
ptp.p2: “Possible unbundling” is our name for two lines on your bill that match one of these edits. It is not a CMS term.
ptp.p3: It is a question to ask the billing office, not a finding that anyone did something wrong.

decides.q: Does Unbundle decide that a charge is wrong?
decides.p1: No. The AI reads your bill into structured data. Fixed, tested rules decide every finding, using public Medicare data, and the AI cannot add, remove or change a finding or its amount.
decides.p2: Separately, if you open “What is this?” on a line, the AI gives a general definition of that billing code. It does not explain or decide your findings.
decides.p3: Findings are things worth asking about, not certain mistakes. One check compares prices with Medicare, and the 5 times threshold it uses is our own choice, not a legal standard.
